originalTitle: Jefferies stays bullish on S&P 500, sees 9,000 by end-2027
summary: Investing.com -- Jefferies expects the S&P 500 to extend its gains through the end of 2026 and into next year, arguing that stronger-than-expected corporate earnings and continued artificial intelligence investment can outweigh risks from inflation, higher oil prices and elevated bond yields.
content:
Investing.com -- Jefferies expects the S&P 500 to extend its gains through the end of 2026 and into next year, arguing that stronger-than-expected corporate earnings and continued artificial intelligence investment can outweigh risks from inflation, higher oil prices and elevated bond yields.

Still guessing which names to buy? Our AI rebuilds its stock picks at the start of every month. The list is beating the market by 120%. See what's on it »

The brokerage set an 8,000 year-end target for the S&P 500 in 2026, based on a forecast of 35% earnings growth and $373 in earnings per share, compared with consensus expectations for 29% growth. It sees the index reaching 9,000 by the end of 2027, supported by $450 in EPS and 20.8% earnings growth.

Jefferies said the earnings outlook has improved sharply this year, with consensus 2026 earnings growth rising from about 13% at the start of the year to 29%. The improvement is also broadening beyond the so-called Magnificent 7, with earnings expectations for the rest of the S&P 500 rising to about 24% for 2026.

AI remains central to the earnings story. Jefferies estimates that companies with direct or indirect exposure to AI and data-centre investment account for about 46% of the S&P 500, with their earnings expected to grow about 60% in 2026. That growth is projected to slow to 24% in 2027, but the brokerage expects both AI-related companies and the rest of the index to continue delivering double-digit earnings growth.

The brokerage said the market's valuation remains elevated but is increasingly supported by the earnings outlook. The S&P 500 trades at about 21.5 times forward earnings, while Jefferies expects its 2027 target to be based on a lower 20-times multiple, meaning its bullish outlook does not depend on significant valuation expansion.

Should you buy NVIDIA right now? Before you decide, consider this: an AI-powered list of stock picks is outperforming the market by 120%, and it updates at the start of every month. See this month's picks »

Higher Treasury yields remain a key risk. Jefferies noted that the 10-year Treasury yield has already risen by more than 60 basis points this year and said historically, a rise of more than 100 basis points over 12 months has been associated with a contraction in equity-market multiples. Rising fiscal deficits and increased debt issuance by large technology companies could add further upward pressure on long-term yields.

Jefferies also expects the market to broaden beyond mega-cap technology. It said only about 36% of S&P 500 stocks were outperforming the index over the 12 months through August, well below the long-term average of about 47%. However, stronger earnings growth across sectors could improve market breadth as investors shift their focus toward 2027.

Among sectors, Jefferies is overweight technology, financials, health care and materials. Technology is expected to post the strongest earnings growth, while financials could benefit from higher long-term rates and capital-markets activity. Health care is one of the few sectors where earnings growth is expected to accelerate in 2027, while materials could benefit from stronger commodity prices.

The brokerage is more cautious on communication services, consumer discretionary and real estate, citing weaker earnings or revision trends, high valuations, slowing consumer confidence and sensitivity to higher interest rates.

Jefferies' 2027 scenarios span a wide range, with a base-case target of 9,000, a bear case of 6,900 and a bull case of 10,500. The report says the main downside risk to its outlook would be a meaningful deterioration in earnings expectations, particularly among AI-related companies.
